title: Careers Education
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman, reflecting on a university open day with his teenage daughter, argues that schools chronically underinvest in the foundational, whole-cohort layer of careers education. His core insight is that careers guidance is a knowledge problem before it is an access problem: a young person cannot express interest in a career they don't know exists, and most students' career knowledge is limited to jobs they have personally seen modeled by family or media. Ashman borrows the tiered Response to Intervention/MTSS framework used for literacy and behaviour interventions and applies it to careers advice, arguing that many schools skip straight to resource-intensive Tier 3 individual interviews without ever building systematic Tier 1 exposure for the whole cohort. He proposes a Tier 1 careers curriculum, delivered informally through assemblies rather than as a dedicated subject, that deliberately introduces students to career sectors they have little personal contact with, and critiques the common substitute of inviting alumni guest speakers, which depends on staff networks and often assumes background knowledge students don't have. The piece closes by subordinating the whole argument to a larger claim about the purpose of schooling: education is not simply preparation for work, and no amount of careers guidance excuses a school that fails to teach students to read, write, and do arithmetic.
points: Ashman reframes careers education as a knowledge problem, not just an access problem: students can't express interest in careers they don't know exist, so exposure has to be systematic rather than incidental.

He borrows the Response to Intervention/MTSS tiering model from literacy and behaviour interventions and applies it to careers advice, arguing most schools jump straight to expensive Tier 3 individual interviews without a Tier 1 foundation.
His proposed Tier 1 is a planned, sequenced curriculum of basic career exposure delivered in assemblies, deliberately skewed toward careers students have had little personal contact with.

He critiques the common practice of inviting former-student guest speakers as Tier 1 instruction, since it depends on staff's personal networks and speakers tend to pitch above students' actual background knowledge.

He subordinates the whole argument to a broader claim: education is not simply job preparation, and a school that nailed careers guidance but failed to teach literacy and numeracy would still have failed.
quotes: When a young person does not even know that a particular kind of job exists, it is impossible for them to express interest in it.

I began to reflect on the Response to Intervention model (also known as Multi-Tiered Systems of Support) we use at my school for guiding interventions in literacy, numeracy, behaviour and other areas. This begins with good Tier 1 instruction for all students.

All students are taught a deliberately planned and sequenced curriculum that gives the basics of a wide range of careers in different sectors, with a deliberate skew towards rewarding careers that students may have had little personal contact with.

Firstly, the curriculum is now dependent on the personal connections of people who work at the school or for the careers advice service. So, students will not necessarily be exposed to the widest range of relevant careers.

Education is not simply preparation for work. It is a deeper process of developing knowledge of the world that may well make young people more employable, but that will also give them a fulfilling life and a cultural hinterland.
I knew about jobs I had seen. I knew about teaching and being a doctor. I knew about engineering because my dad was an engineer.
